description: OXIEDO is building Flame Ledger, an SI-powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's ISS combustion investigations from the PSI database. We rebuilt 126 of 129 BASS-II flame tests run by run, ranked 24 PSI investigations for a Moon-habitat atmosphere, and built a Claude interpreter that answers only with verbatim citations or refuses. Interests: spacecraft fire safety, open science data, and AI for science.
summary:
A Moon base will likely breathe thinner air with a bigger share of oxygen, which NASA's challenge notes makes materials much more flammable. Flame Ledger summarizes and ranks 24 NASA combustion investigations for that air, and answers questions with an AI that must quote its sources word for word, or say "Not in the PSI dataset or indexed NASA reports."

What it shows: for a proposed lunar habitat air of 34% oxygen by volume at 8.2 psia, the ISS study our ranker puts first, BASS-II, has a recorded oxygen range that tops out at 22.2% by volume, in tests at about 1 atm (partial pressures are not compared). None of the solid-fuel cards with a recorded O2 range reaches 34%.

It also shows how one published Moon-gravity estimate leans on an input its own paper calls "not determined in this paper" (ICES-2025-392 p. 10; the paper calls its 35 cm/s value "a conservatively high estimate"). Slide that input across published values and watch the estimate move.

How we checked it: we rebuilt NASA's BASS-II flame-test data run by run from three NASA sources, and every plotted point opens the table cell and report page it came from. Scored blind on a 30-run reference set: 99 of 110 fields correct.

Evidence and sensitivity views, not predictions.
details:
Flame Ledger shows what NASA's space combustion experiments already tell us about fire in the air a Moon base may breathe, and where that evidence stops. It is a five-tab web dashboard built on NASA data, and every plotted point, table value and citation opens the source it came from.

Why it matters: NASA's challenge text says Moon-base air will likely be 30% oxygen or more, at 10.2 psi or less, which makes materials much more flammable; and PSI holds no partial-gravity combustion data yet (challenge text). Anyone choosing materials for that base has to work out which existing tests apply, and how far. Flame Ledger puts the evidence for that question on one screen.

WHAT YOU CAN DO WITH IT

The five tabs are Brief, Rebuild, Explorer, Ranker and Interpreter.

Summarize: 24 investigation cards, built from PSI's own records (objectives, fuels, test conditions, publications, people). Each card carries a short AI summary, and a summary sentence stays only if every quote it cites is found verbatim in its source. One investigation, BASS-II (PSI-25), is rebuilt run by run from three NASA sources: the PSI experimental table, the appendix tables of the NASA test report (NASA/TM-20210011385) and the MSG fan calibration workbook. The rebuild is plotted as the flammability "U-curve": oxygen at the flame limit against the flow stretch on the flame. It shows 17 flame limits from 16 runs.

Rank: pick a mission atmosphere (ISS cabin, lunar habitat, lunar alternate atmosphere, pressurized rover or Mars habitat). All 24 investigations are scored by how closely their evidence matches it, across six features:

- O2 overlap (weight 0.1)

- total-pressure overlap (0.1)

- fuel class (0.2)

- flow regime (0.2)

- fire-safety role (0.2)

- gravity relevance (0.2)

Every point of score names the card field it came from, and missing evidence scores zero and says so. The weights are adjustable. The score ranks how relevant the evidence is; it is not a hazard rating.

Interpret: ask a question in plain English. Claude calls tools over the same JSON files the dashboard renders, and every sentence it writes must carry a citation. On the server, a deterministic check deletes any sentence whose quote is not found verbatim in a source returned during that conversation. If nothing survives, the answer is exactly: "Not in the PSI dataset or indexed NASA reports." Five cached answers work with no live call.

Check any number: click any plotted point, table value or citation, and a receipt opens: the source file, its SHA-256 hash, the exact locator (CSV row and column, PDF page and table, spreadsheet cell) and the verbatim quote.

WHAT IT FOUND

1. The top-ranked ISS evidence sits far below Moon-base oxygen. For the lunar habitat preset (34% O2 at 8.2 psia, from a NASA evidence report on the exploration atmosphere, NTRS 20150021491), the top-ranked investigation is BASS-II. Its recorded O2 range tops out at 22.2 vol%, 11.8 points below the preset, both by volume. No pressure correction is applied. It is not alone: the other solid-fuel cards with a recorded O2 range (SAFFIRE-I and -II) also stop near 22%, while four gas and droplet cards span 34% (ACME BRE, ACME Flame Design, FLEX (PSI-69, not FLEX-2), CFI-G).

2. One published Moon-gravity estimate leans on an input its own paper flags. A 2025 NASA-led paper on solid-fuel ignition for lunar applications (ICES-2025-392) estimates a shift it intends to be conservative in a material's oxygen limit from 1 g to lunar gravity. It uses a "compensation factor": the paper's "worst-case 95% confidence interval slope" (p. 10) of the 1 g extinction limit against forced flow, multiplied by an assumed buoyant velocity, U_b (the updraft a flame makes on Earth). The paper uses 35 cm/s. Its own paper calls that speed "not determined in this paper" (ICES-2025-392 p. 10), and states that "35 cm/s could be considered to be a conservatively high estimate" (p. 10).

Panel B lets you drag U_b across three published values:

- 17 cm/s, the rod-tip stretch equivalent from ICES-2017-370 (a different geometry)

- 20 cm/s, from Hirano (a thin combustible solid, a different geometry)

- 35 cm/s, from Takahashi, as used in the paper

The live readout recomputes the factor for PMMA. At 35 cm/s our arithmetic gives 1.96 O2 percentage points, shown beside the paper's printed 1.9 (Table 2). At 17 cm/s it gives 0.95. Values away from 35 cm/s are this project's arithmetic and are labelled so. The paper's own centrifuge result for PMMA found the lunar-gravity limit "to be less than the extrapolated value (for any assumed buoyant velocity)" (p. 9).

Panel C lists the paper's printed factors for six materials, with the centrifuge sign quoted for five of them (the paper states none for Beefy-T smolder). A second route, the zero-stretch extrapolation from ICES-2017-370, has its own separate input, so the two methods never share a slider. Its K = 1.44 variant was calibrated on the same BASS-II boundary, so it is not independent; the 17 cm/s mark comes from that same fit.

This shows how much a published method leans on one input its own paper did not determine. It is not a prediction, a margin or a certification.

3. The rebuild lands where NASA's own fit does (a consistency check). The lowest flame limit in the rebuilt data is 13.6% O2 (the final chamber reading), at BASS-II run O4: row 51 of the PSI-25 table, joined to Table A.5 of the test report. The report's fitted flammability boundary bottoms out near 13.5% O2 (both by volume). We report this value as found; it was not tuned. It is not a discovery: NASA's fit comes from the same runs, so a rebuild that read the raw table correctly should land here, and it does. O4's flow is below the fan calibration's range, so its flow is only bounded, and the point does not place the bottom of the U.

HOW WE CHECKED IT (SHOWN IN THE PRODUCT)

- Gold-30: 30 BASS-II runs, chosen with a fixed seed (20 random, stratified by PI, plus 10 purposive), giving 110 scored fields. Scored blind on a 30-run reference set: 99 of 110 fields correct.

- Rules-only baseline: 88 of 110 fields correct (80.0%; Wilson 95% interval 71.6–86.4%).

- Rules plus AI, blind: 99 of 110 (90.0%; 83.0–94.3%).

- After adjudicating the 11 disagreements: 100 of 110 (90.9%; 84.1–95.0%). The disagreements are listed in the repository.

- Join: 126 of 129 PSI-table runs matched to the test report appendix (O20, O21 and O22 unmatched), with 0 key conflicts.

- Accuracy gate: set at 80% before scoring; passed.

- Tests: 165 Python tests; 65 front-end tests; narration tests; and a browser test that plays the film and asserts that every number it shows matches the page.

HOW IT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE

- "Summarizes, ranks, and interprets": the Explorer, Ranker and Interpreter tabs, joined on the Brief.

- "Investigations most relevant to ... spacecraft, space stations, bases on the lunar and Martian surfaces, and pressurized rovers": the Ranker's five mission presets cover a space-station cabin, two lunar atmospheres (a habitat and an alternate), a pressurized rover and a Mars habitat.

- "Extract data that supports predictive modeling": the BASS-II rebuild, with every value carrying its source and locator. We extract; we do not model or predict.

- "Research that informs ... fire safety controls and equipment": fire-safety role is a ranking feature, and the Brief links to the suppression (FLEX) and smoke-detection (SAME, SAME-R) records.

- "Fire safety on Earth": the Brief quotes the challenge's examples (ISS water-mist extinguishers, smoke detection, firefighter gear) and links the related PSI records, labelled as related, not as the source of those technologies.

- "No partial-gravity combustion data available in PSI": the Ranker and Panels B and C show where the evidence stops and how a published 1 g-to-lunar method responds to its buoyant-velocity input, which that paper did not determine.

WHO IT'S FOR

- A habitat materials engineer: which space fire evidence reaches a candidate Moon-base atmosphere, and how much one published Moon-gravity estimate moves with an input its own paper did not determine.

- A PSI researcher: the BASS-II flame-test data rebuilt run by run, with each plotted point opening the table cell and report page it came from.

HOW IT'S BUILT

- Offline Python pipeline: it hashes every downloaded NASA file and refuses to run if a hash changes. It parses the PSI table, the test report's appendix tables (pdfplumber) and the fan calibration (openpyxl), and joins them by run. Deterministic rules come first. Only the rows the rules cannot resolve go to Claude, which must return an exact source quote for every value it fills. A value is kept only if a string match finds that quote verbatim in the named source cell. Every value carries its provenance, and an anomaly log records every abstention and conflict.

- Static JSON, checked against a schema before it is written: records, limit points, cards, rankings, sensitivity routes and an index of 476 NASA report and PSI passages.

- A React front end that reads only that JSON, so every number on screen is a value in a file with a receipt.

- One serverless function for the live Interpreter. The API key stays server-side, and spending is capped: at most 3 model calls per answer and 1,500 output tokens per call, plus per-IP and daily limits.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

- Python (3.11+): pydantic, jsonschema, pdfplumber, openpyxl, python-docx, pytest, the Anthropic Python SDK.

- TypeScript: React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS 4, Plotly.js, MiniSearch, the Anthropic TypeScript SDK.

- Hosting: Vercel (static site plus one serverless function).

- Film: Playwright, ffmpeg, Web Audio and ElevenLabs text-to-speech.

HONEST LIMITS

- No Moon prediction, safety margin, certification or material pass/fail. Partial-gravity readouts are sensitivity views, not forecasts.

- Factor values are only printed at 35 cm/s. Every value at another U_b is this project's arithmetic. 17, 20 and 35 cm/s are published values, not a physical range.

- The ~1.9-point similarity is coincidental. The BASS-II microgravity minimum (about 13.5%) against the 15.4% 1 g upward limit with 4 cm/s forced flow (both by volume, both from NASA/TM-20210011385) gives a gap of about 1.9 points, and so does the PMMA compensation factor. They are different quantities, and the similarity is coincidental.

- O2 is compared by volume only. The BASS-II report's O2 bookkeeping uses P = 1 atm (TM p. 11); the lunar preset is 8.2 psia. No pressure correction is applied, so O2 partial pressures are not compared.

- Three presets are assumptions. ISS cabin, pressurized rover and Mars habitat are labelled "assumed" on screen. The lunar habitat and lunar alternate presets are sourced.

- Ranking weights are our choice.

- The cleaned BASS-II dataset has not had expert review. It is a candidate contribution pending expert review; no combustion scientist has reviewed it.

- Three BASS-II runs did not join. O4's flow is only bounded.

- One known misread. Run O12 failed to ignite at 13.6% O2 (start), but the rebuild's reader misreads it as an extinction, so it has no plotted point; the reference-set score counts it as an error, and the Interpreter's cached answer says so.

- The Interpreter knows only its indexed sources: the 24 cards, the BASS-II records, and passages from four NASA papers plus PSI records. A fifth paper (Olson & T'ien) is cited in Panel B but isn't indexed, because its scanned text is unreadable.

- Not a basis for operational decisions. It does not support ventilation, detector or suppression decisions, or material approval.

Team OXIEDO (Dhaka): Rokib Al Dhin Raadh (team owner) and Tanha Mahazabin.

USE OF AI (SI)

Flame Ledger's AI must quote NASA sources word for word. Any sentence whose quote cannot be found in a source is deleted before you see it, and if nothing survives, it says "Not in the PSI dataset or indexed NASA reports."

Where AI runs inside the product:

- Live Interpreter: Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5), in a tool-use loop over the dashboard's own data, with at most 3 model calls per answer and 1,500 output tokens per call. The model must cite a source id and an exact quote for every sentence. A deterministic server check keeps a sentence only if its quote appears verbatim in a source a tool returned in that conversation. The model gets one retry with the reasons; after that, the answer is the refusal string. The project's guardrails are embedded verbatim in the system prompt, and a pattern check blocks banned claims, such as calling a 1 g limit a "MOC".

- Cached answers: four were written by Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and one by Claude Sonnet 5.5. Each names its model on screen, and each passed the same quote check.

- Card summaries: 24, written by Claude Opus 5.5. A sentence stays only if every quote it cites is found verbatim.

- Data pipeline reconcile step: Claude Opus 5.5, only for BASS-II rows the rules could not resolve. A value is kept only if its quote is found verbatim in the named source cell and the value appears inside that quote; otherwise it stays empty, with the reason logged. On the 110 gold fields this lifted accuracy from 88 to 99.

Refusal by design: when the indexed sources do not answer a question, or part of one, the dashboard says "Not in the PSI dataset or indexed NASA reports." It does not guess. If the live service is down, it says so instead of printing the refusal, so an outage never reads as "not in the data".

SI disclosure: Code written with AI coding assistance; the 30-run reference labels were drafted by AI from source text and reviewed by the author; the film's narration voice is AI-generated (ElevenLabs). Some code reuses the author's own prior work (see "References").

The film: recorded from the live site playing itself; the music is generated in code with Web Audio.

NASA DATA USED

Flame Ledger is built on NASA data: 24 combustion investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database, the raw BASS-II data files, and seven papers and reports from NASA's Technical Reports Server (NTRS). Every card, plotted point and ranking traces back to one of the sources below.
